These three are typical of the modern production, 'Italian style' auto knives:

http://i.imgur.com/0QAWCoB.jpg

The little green one is my very first auto knife, marked '440 Stainless Milano'. Both the little dark-horn one, and the big olive-wood version are marked 'Stiletto Italy'. These have been made by a variety of makers over the years, and I have no idea who made any of mine.

These knives are easy to dismiss. The blades are generally made of indifferent steel, which hardly matters because the profile is usually so thick that slicing is impossible anyway. The larger components are hollow, stamped metal, everything is held together with pins that are always a little too proud, and the safeties are never tight enough to be reliable. They give the impression that they are one-use implements which would never be quite the same if ever jammed into something with any real force.

That said, each of my examples opens smartly and securely, with no blade play - none! - in any direction. The blades are centered when closed and the dangerously proud firing buttons are positive and smooth. Despite my every expectation, they work quite well. They are toys, but they are pretty nice toys, despite their humble materials and design. The little green one served admirably as a letter opener during a few of my younger years. I recall tightening the blade pivot, once, by tapping it down with a kitchen spoon.

http://i.imgur.com/8z9RYJU.jpg

Many of course are not quite up to the same quality standard, and I've handled more than a few which were worse in every respect. But most, especially if purchased new, are put together surprisingly well. Be aware that there are now many Chinese copies which, in my experience, are uniformly bad, but of course I might reconsider that judgement if it turns out that one of mine was made there.

Many folks who first encounter these knives are puzzled by how to close them. There is a tiny metal plate on the back of the knife, over the gap between the handle and the blade. This plate needs to be lifted in order to unlock the blade for closing.

Older-style knives, called 'picklocks', required the user to pinch this little plate with the fingertips and lift. The more modern version, generally referred to as 'bolster-release', are cleverly designed to allow one bolster to rotate under thumb pressure, lifting the plate for you:

http://i.imgur.com/yl4QyiN.jpg

(In the interests in keeping the terminology as confusing as possible, note that the phrase 'bolster-release' is also applied to auto knives with no visible firing button, which are instead fired, rather than unlocked, by rotating a bolster in a similar fashion).

These are widely available and come in a bewildering variety of blade styles, handle materials, and sizes. Any of the ones made by the leading Italian makers are probably a pretty good bet. There's a nice selection of them offered here:

http://www.bladeplay.com/cat--Italian-Style-Knives--57
